title: Bitcoin whitepaper: transactions and peer-to-peer timestamping
text: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer electronic cash system. Transactions are digitally signed, broadcast to the network, and timestamped by including them in a proof-of-work chain. Nodes accept blocks by validating their consensus rules, rather than relying on a central operator.

title: Bitcoin Developer Guide: block chain
text: The block chain is a public record of confirmed transactions. Each block references its predecessor, creating an ordered history. Full nodes independently validate blocks and transactions against their consensus rules.
license: Bitcoin Developer Documentation terms; verify before redistribution

title: Bitcoin Developer Guide: mining
text: Mining is the process of constructing candidate blocks and performing proof of work. Miners search for a block header hash below the network target. Proof of work makes rewriting confirmed history computationally expensive, while nodes still independently validate the block rules.

title: Bitcoin Developer Guide: wallets
text: A Bitcoin wallet manages keys and creates transactions. A wallet does not contain bitcoins; it stores or manages the information needed to spend outputs recorded on the blockchain. A seed phrase or private key must be kept secret.

title: Bitcoin Improvement Proposals
text: Bitcoin Improvement Proposals describe proposed standards, processes, and information for the Bitcoin ecosystem. A proposal's status and adoption must be checked individually; publication does not mean a proposal is active consensus policy.

title: Bitcoin Developer Guide: transactions and UTXOs
text: A Bitcoin transaction consumes previously created unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs) as inputs and creates new outputs. Each input references an earlier output, and each output specifies conditions for spending it. A transaction's fee is the difference between input value and output value; nodes validate value conservation and scripts under consensus rules.

title: Bitcoin Developer Guide: peer-to-peer network
text: Bitcoin nodes communicate over a peer-to-peer network to discover peers and exchange blockchain and transaction data. Peer connectivity is a transport and propagation mechanism; a node must still independently validate received blocks and transactions rather than trust a peer's claims.

title: Bitcoin Developer Guide: payment processing
text: Payment systems should treat a transaction's appearance in the mempool as provisional, not equivalent to irreversible settlement. Confirmation depth, transaction replacement, fee conditions, and the value at risk affect payment acceptance policy. A merchant should define explicit confirmation requirements for its threat model.

title: Bitcoin Developer Guide: operating modes
text: Bitcoin software can operate with different levels of validation and data retention. A fully validating node independently checks consensus rules, while lightweight approaches trade some independent verification and privacy for lower resource requirements. The security properties depend on the specific mode and trust assumptions.

title: Bitcoin Core: project overview and license
text: Bitcoin Core is the reference implementation's widely used full-node software project. Its repository describes software that connects to the peer-to-peer network and fully validates blocks and transactions. The Bitcoin Core repository identifies its software license as MIT; this statement does not automatically license unrelated Bitcoin documentation or third-party content.

title: BIP 32: hierarchical deterministic wallets
text: BIP 32 specifies hierarchical deterministic wallets: a tree of keys derived from a master key and derivation paths. Extended keys encode key material and derivation information, enabling structured wallet backup and address generation. Extended public keys are sensitive privacy data even though they cannot directly spend funds.

title: BIP 39: mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys
text: BIP 39 describes converting computer-generated entropy into a human-readable mnemonic and using that mnemonic with an optional passphrase to derive a seed. A mnemonic is a high-value secret: anyone who obtains it and any required passphrase may be able to recover wallet keys. The BIP's proposal status and wallet compatibility should be checked rather than assumed.
license: Check Copyright section of this individual BIP before reuse

title: BIP 141: segregated witness
text: BIP 141 defines Segregated Witness (SegWit), which separates witness data from the traditional transaction serialization and introduces block weight accounting. SegWit changes transaction structure and enables related improvements; fee estimation must account for virtual size rather than treating every serialized byte identically.
license: Check Copyright section of this individual BIP before reuse

title: BIP 341: Taproot consensus layer
text: BIP 341 specifies Taproot's consensus rules, including pay-to-Taproot outputs and spending paths using Schnorr signatures or script paths. Taproot can improve flexibility and privacy in some spending constructions, but it does not make every Bitcoin transaction indistinguishable or guarantee anonymity.
license: Check Copyright section of this individual BIP before reuse

title: BIP 342: validation of Taproot scripts
text: BIP 342 defines validation rules for Tapscript, the script version used by Taproot script-path spends. It works with Taproot's witness structure and signature rules; implementation details and consensus behavior should be checked against the current deployed specification and software version.
license: Check Copyright section of this individual BIP before reuse

title: BIP 174: partially signed Bitcoin transactions
text: BIP 174 defines a standardized format for exchanging partially signed Bitcoin transactions. PSBTs let multiple devices or participants coordinate transaction construction and signing without sharing private keys. A PSBT is not automatically safe: signers must independently verify inputs, outputs, amounts, fees, and change before signing.

title: BOLT 1: base protocol
text: BOLT 1 describes foundational Lightning Network peer-to-peer communication concepts, including message framing and transport-level behavior. Lightning nodes exchange protocol messages over authenticated connections; protocol conformance and implementation security matter independently of Bitcoin base-layer consensus.
license: CC BY 4.0 for the BOLTs specification repository; attribution required

title: BOLT 2: peer protocol for channel management
text: BOLT 2 specifies Lightning peer messages and state transitions used to establish, manage, and close payment channels. Channel operations depend on both peers maintaining consistent protocol state and on on-chain transactions for enforcement and settlement. A channel is not simply an ordinary Bitcoin payment sent to a recipient.
license: CC BY 4.0 for the BOLTs specification repository; attribution required

title: BOLT 7: routing gossip protocol
text: BOLT 7 specifies Lightning gossip messages used to distribute channel and node announcements and routing information. Gossip data helps nodes construct payment routes, but advertised channel information can be stale or incomplete and does not guarantee that a payment will succeed or that liquidity is available in the required direction.
license: CC BY 4.0 for the BOLTs specification repository; attribution required

title: BOLT 11: invoice protocol
text: BOLT 11 defines a Lightning invoice format that communicates payment details such as amount and payment hash, along with other invoice metadata. An invoice is a payment request, not proof that a payment has been completed. Applications must validate expiry, amount, network, and payment result.
license: CC BY 4.0 for the BOLTs specification repository; attribution required

title: BOLT 12: offers
text: BOLT 12 specifies reusable Lightning offers and related messages for requesting and making payments. Offers are distinct from one-time invoices and involve additional protocol flows. Support and behavior can vary by implementation and version, so integrations should check current specification status and implementation compatibility.
